fresh_description: Fresh Willamette Valley strawberries — in season mid-May through late June
yield_ratio: 4 cups sliced strawberries + rhubarb and sugar yield about 10 half-pint jars preserves
why_preserve: Preserving strawberries as jam extends their enjoyment well beyond the short fresh season.
fun_talking_point: A good strawberry-rhubarb preserve can yield 10 half-pint jars from 4 cups each of fruit.
info_card_text: Strawberries paired with tart rhubarb make a perfect balance in homemade preserves. Follow safe water bath canning steps to preserve freshness and flavor for winter enjoyment.
source_excerpt: Preserve Recipes Strawberry - Rhubarb Preserves (about 10 half-pint jars) • 4 cups sliced rhubarb • 4 cups strawberries • 7 cups sugar. Slowly bring to a boil, cook rapidly until thick. Process in boiling water canner.

fresh_description: Fresh, young Willamette Valley green beans — peak harvest July to September
yield_ratio: 1½ to 2½ pounds of beans per quart jar; about 12–20 quarts from 30 pounds (1 bushel)
why_preserve: Canning green beans extends their use and provides cooked beans ready for meals.
fun_talking_point: One bushel of fresh green beans yields up to 20 quarts of canned beans.
info_card_text: Canning green beans requires pressure canning to ensure safety. Use young, tender beans and pack them hot or raw into jars. Follow the exact processing times for altitude.
source_excerpt: It takes about 1½ to 2½ pounds of beans to fill a quart jar. Beans must be processed in a pressure canner at 240°F.

fresh_description: Fresh Willamette Valley freestone peaches — in season July through September
yield_ratio: 2 to 3 pounds fresh peaches per quart jar; about 18–24 quarts per bushel (48 pounds)
why_preserve: Canning peaches locks in the sweet flavor for winter desserts and snacks.
fun_talking_point: Canning peaches in syrup helps them hold shape and quality better than raw pack.
info_card_text: Freestone yellow peaches are preferred for home canning. Peel, pit, slice and pack in syrup before processing in boiling water canner. Do not can white-flesh peaches due to safety concerns.
source_excerpt: It takes about 2 - 3 pounds of peaches to fill a quart jar. Peaches must be processed in a boiling water canner. Peaches canned with syrup will hold their shape better.

fresh_description: Fresh Willamette Valley cucumbers — in season June through August
yield_ratio: About 10 pounds cucumbers to 9 pints pickles
why_preserve: Pickling cucumbers enhances flavor and preserves texture for months.
fun_talking_point: Home pickled cucumbers combine vinegar, salt, and spices for a tangy, crunchy treat.
info_card_text: Pickled cucumbers can be safely canned using tested recipes with vinegar acid levels to prevent spoilage. Use fresh crisp cucumbers and process in boiling water canner.
source_excerpt: Pickling of vegetables using vinegar and salt preserves the product safely and adds flavor.

fresh_description: Fresh Willamette Valley raspberries — in season June through July
yield_ratio: 2 pounds fresh raspberries freeze to about 2 pounds frozen berries
why_preserve: Freezing preserves fresh flavor and nutrients for year-round use.
fun_talking_point: Raspberries can be frozen whole or as purée with ascorbic acid to maintain color and flavor.
info_card_text: Select ripe, juicy raspberries; wash gently and drain. Pack individually quick-frozen or in syrup. Use within a year for best quality.
source_excerpt: Raspberries select fully ripe juicy berries. Wash and drain. Pack in syrup or without sugar.

fresh_description: Fresh Willamette Valley tomatoes — in season July through September
yield_ratio: About 2½ to 3 pounds tomatoes per quart jar
why_preserve: Canning tomatoes extends their use for sauces and soups throughout the year.
fun_talking_point: Adding bottled lemon juice ensures safe acidity for canned tomatoes.
info_card_text: Select ripe, firm tomatoes; blanch and peel. Pack in hot water or juice with lemon juice to ensure safe pH. Process in boiling water canner with recommended time.
source_document: PNW 300 Canning tomatoes and tomato products
source_excerpt: Tomatoes may be canned in boiling water canner if acidified with bottled lemon juice or citric acid.

fresh_description: Fresh Willamette Valley zucchini — in season July through September
yield_ratio: About 1 pound fresh zucchini yields about 1 pound frozen zucchini
why_preserve: Freezing zucchini keeps it fresh for soups, stews, and casseroles through winter.
fun_talking_point: Blanch zucchini slices for 3 minutes before freezing to retain flavor and texture.
info_card_text: Trim, wash, slice zucchini. Blanch in boiling water for 3 minutes, cool in ice water, drain, and pack in freezer containers. Label and use within one year.
source_excerpt: Blanch zucchini slices for 3 minutes. Cool, drain, pack and freeze.

fresh_description: Fresh Willamette Valley basil — harvest July through September
yield_ratio: About 6 cups fresh leaves yield 1 cup dried herbs
why_preserve: Drying intensifies basil flavor and provides herbs year-round for cooking.
fun_talking_point: Basil can be dried using kitchen dehydrators or air drying in shaded, airy space.
info_card_text: Harvest fresh basil leaves, wash, and dry quickly. Spread thinly to dry. Store in airtight containers away from light and heat for up to one year.
source_excerpt: Drying herbs concentrates their flavors and preserves them for extended use.

fresh_description: Fresh Willamette Valley apples — peak season September through November
yield_ratio: About 2 to 3 pounds apples per quart jar
why_preserve: Canning apples captures fall harvest flavor for winter desserts and snacks.
fun_talking_point: Adding lemon juice to apple slices prevents browning prior to packing.
info_card_text: Select crisp apples. Peel, core, and slice. Prepare a boiling syrup and pack apples hot. Process in boiling water canner according to recipe.
source_excerpt: Fruit can be canned in water, juice, or syrups using boiling water canner.

fresh_description: Fresh Willamette Valley cherries — peak season June through July
yield_ratio: Approximately 4 cups crushed cherries make 4 half-pint jars jam
why_preserve: Jam preserves fresh cherry flavor and can be enjoyed year-round.
fun_talking_point: Cherries are low in pectin; commercial pectin helps jam gel well.
info_card_text: Crush cherries and cook with sugar and commercial pectin for best results. Pour into hot sterilized jars and process promptly in a water bath canner.
source_excerpt: Jams made with low pectin fruits like cherries require added pectin to gel properly.

fresh_description: Fresh Willamette Valley rhubarb stalks — in season April through June
yield_ratio: About 2 pounds fresh rhubarb yield 2 pounds frozen
why_preserve: Freezing preserves tart rhubarb for baking long after harvest.
fun_talking_point: Rhubarb chunks can be frozen raw or blanched briefly to preserve color.
info_card_text: Wash, trim, and cut into ½-inch pieces. Blanch for 1 minute and cool quickly, or freeze raw. Pack into freezer containers with ½-inch headspace.
source_excerpt: Blanching rhubarb in boiling water for 1 minute retains color and flavor.

fresh_description: Fresh Willamette Valley blueberries — in season July through August
yield_ratio: Approximately 4 cups fresh blueberries yield 1 cup dried blueberries
why_preserve: Drying blueberries concentrates their flavor and provides healthy snacks.
fun_talking_point: Dried blueberries are a natural, shelf-stable ingredient for cereals and baking.
info_card_text: Wash blueberries and dry thoroughly. Use a dehydrator at recommended temperatures until completely dry. Store in airtight containers.
source_excerpt: Drying removes moisture to prevent spoilage and extends shelf life.

fresh_description: Fresh Willamette Valley carrots — available year-round, peak summer-fall
yield_ratio: About 1 pound fresh carrots yields 1 pound frozen carrots
why_preserve: Freezing carrots keeps their flavor and nutrients for winter soups and stews.
fun_talking_point: Carrots require blanching for 5 minutes before freezing to maintain quality.
info_card_text: Wash, peel, and slice carrots. Blanch in boiling water for 5 minutes. Cool rapidly in ice water and pack in freezer containers.
source_excerpt: Blanch carrots for 5 minutes before freezing to preserve texture and color.

fresh_description: Fresh Willamette Valley cabbage — available August through November
yield_ratio: 16 pounds fresh cabbage yields about 1 gallon sauerkraut
why_preserve: Fermentation preserves cabbage for months and creates probiotics.
fun_talking_point: Sauerkraut fermentation produces lactic acid which naturally preserves and adds tangy flavor.
info_card_text: Shred cabbage, mix with salt, and pack tightly in fermentation vessel. Allow to ferment at cool room temperature for 2-4 weeks. Store sauerkraut refrigerated after fermentation.
source_excerpt: Fermentation preserves vegetables by producing acid from salt and naturally occurring bacteria.

fresh_description: Fresh Willamette Valley hot peppers — in season August through October
yield_ratio: 1 pound fresh peppers yields roughly 1 pound frozen
why_preserve: Freezing preserves the heat and flavor of peppers for later cooking.
fun_talking_point: Peppers can be frozen whole or chopped, no blanching required for hot types.
info_card_text: Wash peppers, remove stems and seeds if desired. Chop or freeze whole in bags. Use gloves during preparation.
source_excerpt: Hot peppers can be frozen without heating first and retain flavor and heat.

fresh_description: Fresh Willamette Valley garlic — available summer through fall
yield_ratio: About 10 bulbs fresh garlic yield 1 cup dried flakes
why_preserve: Drying garlic provides long shelf life and concentrated flavor.
fun_talking_point: Dried garlic flakes rehydrate quickly and can be used like fresh garlic.
info_card_text: Peel cloves and slice thinly. Dry in dehydrator until brittle. Store in airtight container away from light and heat.
source_excerpt: Drying is a traditional preservation method that removes moisture to extend shelf life.

fresh_description: Fresh Willamette Valley plums — in season August through September
yield_ratio: Approximately 2 pounds fresh plums per quart jar
why_preserve: Canning plums extends their sweet flavor for use in desserts and sauces.
fun_talking_point: Plums can also be frozen whole or as purée safely.
info_card_text: Wash, pit, and halve plums. Pack in syrup or water with boiling water canner processing times. Use lemon juice as needed to ensure acidity.
source_excerpt: Plums can be canned or frozen; use ascorbic acid to prevent browning.

fresh_description: Fresh Willamette Valley pears — peak season September through November
yield_ratio: Approximately 2 pounds fresh pears per quart jar
why_preserve: Canning pears allows enjoying fall flavors all winter long.
fun_talking_point: Pears should be blanched in boiling syrup before packing to soften and retain quality.
info_card_text: Select firm ripe pears; peel, core, and halve. Heat in boiling syrup, drain, cool and pack in syrup or water before canning.
source_excerpt: Heat in boiling syrup for 1 to 2 minutes before packing pears for freezing or canning.

fresh_description: Fresh Willamette Valley onions — available year-round, peak summer
yield_ratio: About 1 pound fresh onions yield 1 pound frozen onions
why_preserve: Freezing onions saves chopping time and reduces waste.
fun_talking_point: Onions can be frozen raw or blanched for longer storage.
info_card_text: Peel and dice onions. Blanch for 3-7 minutes, cool quickly, drain, and freeze in sealed containers or bags.
source_excerpt: Onions may be frozen diced and unblanched or blanched 3-7 minutes to preserve quality.

fresh_description: Fresh Willamette Valley blackberries—peak season July through August
yield_ratio: 2 cups crushed blackberries yield about 4 half-pint jars jam
why_preserve: Preserving blackberries as jam extends their use beyond the short fresh season, capturing their sweet flavor year-round.
fun_talking_point: Fresh berries yield about half as many quarts when frozen or canned whole, but jams concentrate the flavor and sugar for long-term enjoyment.
info_card_text: Blackberries can be canned whole in syrup or preserved as jam using crushed berries for a thick, spreadable fruit preserve. Use ripe, sweet berries for the best flavor and follow boiling water canning guidelines for safety. Freezing berries in sugar syrup helps retain firmness, but jam is perfect for spreading on toast or adding to desserts.
source_excerpt: 2 lbs. of fresh berries will yield 1 quart of frozen or canned berries; every quart yields approximately 2 cups mashed for jam. Jam is made from crushed fruit and requires water bath canning
